Abstract 
The present study aimed to evaluate effect of Ganoderma atrum polysaccharide (PSG) on acute 
lung injury (ALI) rats and its mechanisms. Results showed that PSG exhibited protective 
effects against ALI by maintaining pulmonary histology, reducing levels of pro-inflammatory 
cytokines and NO both in serum and lung tissue. Moreover, this study further evaluated the 
metabolic effects of PSG based on UPLC-Triple-TOF/MS metabolomics analysis in rats. 
Compared with control group, LysoPC (18:2), LPA (18:1), taurocholic acid, L-histidine, and 
L-tryptophan were identified as metabolic biomarkers in serum of ALI group. Furthermore, 
biological pathways analysis demonstrated that histidine metabolism, nitrogen metabolism, 
tryptophan and part glycerophospholipids metabolism were notably modified by PSG treatment 
in ALI rats. Additionally, improved gut microbial metabolite short-chain fatty acids were 
found after intake of PSG in ALI rat. Altogether, PSG could control ALI-induced aberrant 
inflammation and its mechanisms were linked to inhibit release of pro-inflammatory mediators 
and reverse metabolic pathway disturbances. 
  
Key Words: Gnaoderma atrum polysaccharide; Acute lung injury; Inflammation; Metabolism
1. Introduction 
Studies have demonstrated a critical role for inflammation in immune defense against injury, 
stress and endogenous/exogenous stimuli [1-3]. Nevertheless, defects in inflammation 
elimination and misinterpretation of inflammatory signals could trigger the risk to develop 
acute and chronic inflammatory diseases. Acute lung injury (ALI) is a common inflammatory 
disease and usually associated with various illnesses such as shock, sepsis, and 


 
3 
ischemia-reperfusion giving rise to high morbidity and mortality [4, 5]. Additionally, the 
pathogenesis of ALI refers to multiple factors such as coagulation and fibrinolysis, redox 
imbalance, cell apoptosis, and genetic factors, which are also reported to cause the chaos of 
inflammatory responses [6]. Currently, the non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, such as 
aspirin and phenylbutazone are applied for inflammation treatment [7]. However, their 
adverse effects like gastrointestinal disorders limit their clinical application [8]. Thus, it is still 
necessary to screen new effective strategies for the improvement of ALI.  
Ganoderma atrum, a member of mushroom, has been used extensively as traditional medicine 
or dietary supplements for immune benefits in oriental countries [9, 10]. A polysaccharide 
from Ganoderma atrum (named PSG), the major component was purified from its fruiting 
bodies. The phenol-sulfuric acid assay showed that PSG included PSG-1 (Fig. S1) and PSG-2 
(Fig. S2). PSG-1 was mainly composed of glucose, mannose and galactose with a molecular 
weight of 1013 kDa. Methylation, combined with NMR and GC-MS analysis revealed that its 
main linkage type was β-(1→3)-D-linked-Glcp [11]. Meanwhile, PSG-2 was composed of 
galactose, fucose and glucose with a molecular weight of 69 kDa, and the main linkage type 
was α-(1→6)-Galp [12]. Furthermore, previous studies reported that PSG could control 
lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced aberrant inflammation through alleviating the secretion of 
pro-inflammatory cytokines in macrophage [13]. However, there was no report on whether 
PSG could attenuate inflammation in ALI.  
Metabolomics is an excellent tool to monitor the endogenous small molecule metabolites in 
biological systems, and can efficiently accomplish the quantitative and qualitative 
measurement of metabolites via gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, liquid phase mass 


 
4 
spectrometry, 1H-nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy and capillary electrophoresis mass 
spectroscopy [14, 15]. Therefore, metabolomics could display what occurs in diseases process 
by identifying potential biomarkers and related metabolic pathway. In addition to 
inflammatory responses which are mediated by proinflammatory mediators, metabolism 
disturbances triggers massive pathways cascade expanding inflammation in ALI [16,17]. 
Generally, changes of metabolites are demonstrated in bio-fluid such as plasma, urine and 
spine fluid. A series of studies focusing on inflammatory metabolomics have been reported, 
but few researchers apply metabolomics to assess the anti-inflammatory effects of PSG.  
LPS, a cell wall component of gram-negative bacteria, has been demonstrated to induce 
multiple inflammatory response and release of pro-inflammatory cytokines in lung, and thus 
common applied to establish inflammation-induced lung damage model to mimic ALI in 
clinical settings. Therefore, the aims of this study were to investigate the protective effects of 
PSG in LPS-induced ALI rats via serum metabolic profiling, and to illuminate the metabolic 
pathways and underlying mechanisms of PSG by an untargeted UPLC-Triple-TOF/MS 
metabolomics. 
2. Materials and Methods 
2.1 Chemicals and Reagents 
Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from Escherichia coli 055: B5 was provided by Sigma (St. Louis, 
MO, U.S.A.) and dexamethasone sodium phosphate Injection (DEX) was obtained from 
Henan Runhong Pharmaceutical co. LTD (Xinzheng City, Henan Province, China). For 
UPLC-Triple-TOF/MS analysis, HPLC-grade acetonitrile was purchased from Merck 


 
5 
(Darmstadt, Germany). Ammonium acetate and formic acid were obtained from 
Sigma-Aldrich (St. Luis, MO, USA).  
2.2 Isolation and Chemical Analysis of PSG 
In this experiment, PSG was prepared from fruiting bodies of Ganoderma atrum which was 
cultivated and collected in Dongjiangyuan’s Edible Fungus Factory (Xunwu County, Gannan 
City, Jiangxi Province, China). Subsequently, the shattered and defatted fruiting bodies of 
Ganoderma atrum were extracted with ultrapure water (1:40, w/v) at 90℃ for 2 h twice. The 
aqueous extracts were finally pooled and precipitated in 80% ethanol (v/v) at 4 ℃ to obtain 
the crude Ganoderma atrum polysaccharide. The obtained crude polysaccharide was 
dissolved in ultrapure water and deproteinized by Sevag method for three times. The 
protein-free polysaccharide was subjected to ultrapure water dialysis and precipitated again in 
80% ethanol (v/v) to get the refined polysaccharide (named PSG) [11].  
2.3 Animals and Experimental Design 
Six-weeks-old male Sprague Dawley rats weighing 180-200g, were supplied by Jiangxi 
College of Traditional Chinese Medicine [Jiangxi, China; Grade II, Certificate Number SCXK 
(gan) 2018-0003]. In this study, all animals were housed at constant room temperature 
(222℃) with a regime of 12 h light-dark cycle, freed to receive food and water ad libitum, 
and acclimatized to the laboratory for one week before the experiment.  
After acclimation, sixty rats were randomly divided into six groups (n=10): control, LPS, 
LPS+PSG (20, 40 and 80 mg/kg), LPS+DEX (5mg/kg). ALI model was established by 
intraperitoneal administration (i.p.) of LPS as previously described [18, 23]. Rats were orally 
administered either vehicle (0.9% saline) alone or vehicle composition containing PSG (20, 


 
6 
40, and 80 mg/kg/d) for 7 days. On the seventh day of the experiment, all rats were fasted for 
10 h and then pretreated with PSG, 0.9% saline, via or DEX by i.p. After 30 minutes, LPS (0.8 
mg/kg) were injected into each group, except for the control group. Finally, rats were 
sacrificed 6 h after addition of LPS and samples were harvested. Serum was obtained through 
centrifugation of blood samples at 3000 rpm for 15 min, and stored at -80℃ until biochemical 
analysis.  
Throughout the experiments, all animals care adhere to the NIH Guide for the Care and Use 
of Laboratory Animals, and all experimental procedures were approved by Nanchang 
University Medical College Animal Care Review Committee. 
2.4 Measurement of Visceral index and White Blood Cell Counts (WBC) 
The thymus, spleen, and lung tissues were collected under anaesthetized condition to calculate 
the visceral index. The values were converted to visceral index via the formula: visceral index 
= (organ weight (mg) / the weight of rat (g). The WBC was detected by an automated 
hematology analyzer.  
2.5 Hematoxylin-eosin Staining Analysis of Lung  
The collected lung tissues were used for hematoxylin-eosin staining (H&E) analysis. Briefly, 
lung tissues were routinely fixed in 10% neutral formalin followed by dehydrating, paraffin 
embedding, and slicing. After hematoxylin and eosin staining, pathological changes in the 
lung tissues were viewed under a light microscope (400×) and analyzed according to previous 
studies [19]. 
2.6 Measurement of Cytokine Concentrations 


 
7 
Serum and 10% (w/v) lung homogenate were directly used to determine inflammatory 
mediators including nitric oxide (NO), tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α), interleukin-1β 
(IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6) by commercial rat enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay kits 
purchased from Boster Biological Engineering Co. (Wuhan, Hubei, China). 
2.7 Metabolite Sample Preparation 
The means of serum preparation used in this work was similar to the description reported by 
Zhu et al [20]. Briefly, 100 µL serum samples were diluted with 200 µL liquor with volume of 
4:1 acetonitrile-water (V/V) to precipitate protein. Then samples were vortexed for 1 min, and 
centrifuged at 12 000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C. Finally, the supernatant was collected and 
transferred into a vial after filtering through a 0.22um filter membrane for UPLC–Q-TOF-MS 
analysis. 
2.8 Chromatographic Conditions. 
The UPLC separation was performed on a Shimadzu Nexera X2 UHPLC system (Kyoto, 
Japan) coupled with a Shim-pack GIST C18 column (2.1×75 mm, 2 µm). The column 
temperature was kept at 40 ℃, and 5 µL of each sample solution was injected. The mobile 
phases consisted of a gradient elution with phase A (0.1% formic acid) and phase B 
(acetonitrile modified with 0.1% formic acid) for the positive model, and phase A (5 mm 
ammonium acetate ) and phase B (acetonitrile ) for the negative, for which the flow rate was 
at 0.25ml/min. The gradient elution was applied as follows: 0-2min, 0-5% B; 2-7min, 5-70% 
B; 7-9 min, 80-85% B; 9-11.min,85-89% B;11-12 min, 89-95% B; 12-14 min, 95-95% B, 
14-15 min, 5% B. 
2.9 Mass spectrometry Conditions 


 
8 
For MS/MS, high-resolution mass spectrometry detection of metabolites was performed by an 
AB SCIEX Triple TOF 5600 mass analyzer with information-dependent acquisition (IDA). 
Both positive and negative ionization modes were applied to gather data under a mass range 
100 to 1250 Da. The collision energy was set at 40 V/-40V and with a collision energy spread 
of 10 V. Ion source gas 1 and 2 and curtain gas were set at 50psi, 50psi, and 35psi, 
respectively. The ion spray voltage source was set at 5.5/-5.5KV and the source temperature at 
500°C. Calibration solutions purchased from AB SCIEX were applied to instrument 
calibration. 
2.10 UPLC-Triple-TOF/MS Data Processing  
The original UPLC-MS/MS data were loaded on the Progenesis QI software (Waters, Milford, 
MA, USA), a practical data processing vehicle for omics studies. The general procedure in 
this software involved data import, chromatographic peak alignment, experimental design 
setup, peak picking, normalization, deconvolution, compound identification, and compound 
statistics. The imported 40 runs were aligned based on an automatically selected all samples. 
And the selected adduct ion forms, including [M+H]+, [M+NH4]+, [M+Na]+ in positive mode 
and [M-H]-, [M+Na-2H]-, [M+K-2H]-and [2M+Hac-H]- in negative mode, were applied to 
deconvolute the spectral data.The exported data regarding the retention time, peak intensity, 
and exact mass were then imported to SIMCA-P14.0 (Umetrics AB, Umea, Sweden) for 
multivariate statistical analysis. 
2.11 Measurement of Short Chain Fatty Acids (SCFAs) in Cecum Contents  
The measurement of SCFAs from cecum was carried out according to previous study [16]. 
Briefly, the samples were diluted with ultrapure water at a ratio of 1:7 and mixed on a vortex 


 
9 
mixer for 1 min. The supernatants were obtained with centrifuging at 10000×g for 15 min and 
filtrated for gas chromatography (GC) analysis. The contents of SCFAs were detected by 
Agilent 6890 GC (Agilent Technologies Corp., USA) coupled with a flame ionization detector 
(FID) and a GC column (30 m × 0.32mm, 0.25 mm). Chromatographic analysis was executed 
according to our previous method [21]. 
2.12 Statistical Analysis 
The IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α and NO level of serum and lung were analyzed using SPSS software 
(version 22.0, IBM, Armonk, NY, USA). The data are reported as the means± standard error 
of measurement (SEM). One-way ANOVA followed by Least Significant Difference (LSD) 
test was used to assess the statistical differences. Values of p < 0.05 were considered 
statistically significant. 
3. Results and Discussion 
3.1 Effect of PSG on WBC count in LPS-treated Rats 
WBC (also called Leukocytes) count is well known as a basic parameter to reflect host 
immune response. It is common to know that that WBC count would be increased under 
chronic or acute inflammation conditions [22]. In this work, there was a significant reduction 
of WBC count in LPS group when compared to control group (Table 1). Due to LPS-induced 
the wall-attachment of WBC and myelosuppression, many studies presented similar patterns 
on the decent of WBC count that was found in our results, and suggested that LPS could 
cause the damage of hose immune function. Moreover, compared with LPS group, treatments 
with PSG at the dose 40 and 80 mg/kg BW, respectively, or DEX displayed a significant 


 
10 
increase of WBC count, indicating that PSG could avoid LPS-caused the immune chaos in 
vivo.  
3.2 Effect of PSG on Thymus and Spleen Indexes in LPS-treated Rats 
The thymus and spleen are important immune organs, whose indexes are usually used as an 
index to assess the host immune capability [23]. As shown in Table 1, the thymus and spleen 
indexes increased in rats after treatment with LPS alone, compared with control rats. 
Nevertheless, the enhancements of these indexes after LPS treatment were dramatically 
alleviated by PSG treatment except for PSG at a concentration of 20 mg/kg. Similarly, after 
the treatment of DEX, the spleen index remarkably decreased in rats. It was worth noting that 
the thymus index of DEX group was lower than this observed in control group, suggesting 
that the damage to the thymus might be related to the adverse side effects of DEX. Together, 
these findings suggested that PSG could inhibit the enhancement of thymus and spleen 
indexes in rats subjected to LPS alone. 
3.3 Effect of PSG on Lung Index in LPS-treated Rats 
In the present study, rats exposed to LPS injections showed an increase in lung index 
compared with untreated rats in control group. Our data found that treatment with DEX 
induced a significant reduction in lung index of LPS-treated rats (Table 1). Meanwhile, PSG-1 
resulted in a slight decrease in lung index compared with LPS treatment alone in rats. 
However, there was no significant distinguishment between LPS group and PSG treatment 
groups, indicating that PSG could not completely restore lung injury induced by LPS. Unlike 
DEX, PSG was suggested to be a biological response modifier by strengthening host immune 
defense [24]. Although PSG-1 failed to normalize lung index, the phenomenon might be 


 
11 
partly related to the time limit. In this work, experimental period was short, because 
the experimental measurements were carried out after 6 h LPS treatment. It was hardly for 
PSG to achieve the significant reduction of lung index in the short term response. Accordingly, 
more experiments will be required to confirm those of the treatment with LPS alone or 
together with PSG by extending experimental period such as chronic inflammation study. 
3.4 Effect of PSG on Pathological Changes of Lung in LPS-treated Rats 
H&E analysis was employed to measure morphological alterations of lung tissues, and the 
histological changes of lungs were observed under a light microscope [25]. As depicted in 
Figure 1A, lung of the control rats presented normal lung morphology with a thin alveolar 
wall, and there is no alveolar capillaries congestion and apparent inflammatory cell infiltration. 
Furthermore, LPS treatment showed excessive neutrophils and macrophages infiltration in the 
interstitial tissue. Meanwhile, lung specimen further displayed significant alveolar walls 
thickening and alveolar capillaries congesting indicating pathological injury of lung in LPS 
group. Notably, these lung histopathological changes caused by LPS were significantly 
attenuated by PSG treatment or DEX treatment. These findings indicated that PSG-mediated 
lung protection was associated with the maintenance of lung morphology. 
3.5 Effect of PSG on the Level of Cytokines in LPS-treated Rats 
Inflammation could be characterized by uncontrollably sustained and vigorous inflammatory 
responses. Previous studied have reported that LPS-induced inflammation was involved in 
activation of MAPKs, NF-kB, JAK signal pathway mediated by CD14 or TLR4, thereby 
resulting in overproduction of cytokines such as IL-1β and TNF-ɑ [26, 27]. Liu et al. pointed 
that TNF-ɑ and IL-1β could induce the expression of other cytokines including IL-6, and 


 
12 
increase production of NO [28]. In general, elevated levels of NO and pro-inflammatory 
cytokines were crucial steps and played an important role in the development and progression 
of ALI. Therefore, to further explore the protective effect of PSG against LPS-induced ALI 
rats, the levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β) and NO production 
were detected in serum and lung tissues in this study. Results (Figure 1B-E) showed that the 
levels of these pro-inflammatory cytokines and NO generation in serum of LPS group were 
remarkably higher than those displayed in serum of untreated control group (p<0.05). Notably, 
PSG and DEX pretreatment blocked LPS-induced the enhancement of IL-6, TNF-ɑ, IL-1β 
and NO production in serum in comparison with LPS group. Additionally, consistent with the 
aforementioned results, pulmonary levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokines and NO 
significantly also increased in the LPS group (Figure 1F-I). Furthermore, enhancement of 
pro-inflammatory cytokines and NO were obviously prevented by administration of PSG at a 
dose of 80 mg/kg BW. Meanwhile, DEX also significantly reduced the aforementioned 
parameters except for IL-6. These data illustrated that PSG could protect rats against 
pulmonary inflammation during ALI by suppressing the release of decreasing the 
pro-inflammatory mediators in ALI.  
3.6 Multivariate Statistical Analysis of Serum Metabolite Profiling 
In the above experiments, we investigated the three doses for the effects of PSG on ALI, and 
the dose of 80 mg/kg showed an optimal capacity to protect rats against LPS-induced ALI. 
Accordingly, 80mg/kg was employed for further metabolomics studies. Therefore, the rats 
divided into four groups: the control group (abbreviated as Con), the LPS-treated group 
(abbreviated as LPS), the PSG-treated rats group (80mg/kg, abbreviated as PSG), the 


 
13 
DEX-treated rats group (abbreviated as DEX). After data processing by Progenesis QI, a total 
of 7299 and 7619 spectral features were respectively determined in positive and negative 
mode. Next, these obtained features were used in the multivariate statistical analysis involving 
principal component analysis (PCA), orthogonal partial least squares discrimination 
(OPLS-DA), and heatmap. Briefly, the 3D score plot of PCA presented no significant 
distinction between the Con and LPS groups under the conditions of the negative model, but 
there is an obvious separation trend between LPS group and PSG or DEX group (Figure 2A). 
Meanwhile, the supervised OPLS-DA was further performed to discern the differential 
metabolites between each two groups (Figure 2B) both in the positive and negative modes. 
Results showed that clusters could be remarkably distinguished between the metabolite 
profiles of each of the two groups. And these models R2 and Q2 were listed in Table S1, 
indicating the OPLS-DA models are reliable. Moreover, a permutation test was implemented 
to validate whether the OPLS-DA models were overfitted. All permuted R2 and Q2 values 
were lower than the original values, while the Q2 values were closed to zero, which illustrated 
the robustness of OPLS-DA models and showed a low risk of overfitting and reliability.  
3.7 Identification of Metabolites  
In order to identify difference metabolites between the two groups, the value of variable 
importance in the projection (VIP) >1 in OPLS-DA model was applied to pre-select 
metabolites. These metabolites whose p>0.05 were discarded by between-group comparison. 
According to their molecular weight and tandem mass spectra with METLIN and HMDB 
databases, a total of 33 endogenous metabolites were identified (Table 2). Furthermore, the 
MetaboAnalyst 3.0 platform was applied to form a visualized heat map to exhibit the relative 


 
14 
content of latent biomarkers in each group (Figure 2C). The result demonstrated the variation 
trends of average quantities of these difference metabolites in normal, LPS, PSG and 
DEX-treated rats. Afterward, there were 8 up-regulated metabolites and 6 down-regulated 
metabolites in serum of rat subjected to LPS alone when compared to normal rats. 
Correspondingly, compared with LPS group, 5 endogenous metabolites were up-regulated and 
9 endogenous metabolites were down-regulated after administrating PSG. Moreover, 11 
metabolites were co-owned by PSG group with DEX group in ALI rats (Figure 2D). These 
findings indicated that PSG-triggered protective effects against ALI closely linked to its 
effects on the modification of metabolites changes in rats.  
3.8 Correlation between Changed Metabolites and Serum Mediators of ALI in Rats 
Subjected to LPS Alone. 
Spearman rank correlation analysis was further used to investigate the relationship between 
metabolites (Table 3) and inflammatory mediators including NO, IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-ɑ, and 
finally figured out promising biomarkers. Meanwhile, the mediators and metabolites which 
reached statistical signiﬁcance (p<0.05) in LPS group when compared to Con group were then 
taken to analyze by Metaboanalyst 3.0. Figure 3 displayed that the cytokines IL-1β, IL-6 and 
TNF-ɑ were highly correlated with each other (r>0.91, P<0.01) as well as NO (r>0.40).  
Furthermore, results presented a positive relationship between cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6 and 
TNF-ɑ) and endogenous metabolites (TUCA and TC) (r>0.40). However, LysoPC (18:2), 
LysoPC (20:4) and PC (20:5) were negatively correlated to IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-ɑ (r<-0.6, 
P<0.05), revealing that glycerophospholipids metabolism was strongly related to the 
pathogenesis of ALI caused by LPS in rats. Simultaneously, the NO was in positive 


 
15 
relationship to TUCA and LysoPE (20:4), along with the negative correlation with 
5-CH3-THF. In addition, L-histidine were appeared a high relevance to LysoPE (20:4) , 
LPA(18:1), LysoPC (P-180) and PS (18:1) (r>0.449). Generally, inflammation could be 
triggered by NO and pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-ɑ through activating 
their corresponding pathways [29]. In short, this correlation analysis suggested that the 
changes of metabolites were closely linked to their alternations of biochemical parameters 
such as IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-ɑ and NO, providing the deep meaning of these parameters and 
indirect evidence to understand the pathological mechanisms of LPS-induced ALI. 
3.9 Metabolic Pathway and Function Analysis of PSG 
To identify the potential metabolic pathways that were influenced by LPS, PSG or DEX , we 
next used MetPA-based on the source of the KEGG database to analyze the pathways. In this 
work, the pathway analysis algorithms were set as hypergeometric test for over-representation 
analysis and out-degree centrality for pathway topology analysis. Figure 4 A was the pathway 
analysis between the LPS and Con groups the metabolites showed in Table 3 and displayed 8 
pathways including glycerophospholipid, glycerolipid, taurine and hypotaurine, nitrogen, 
histidine, primary bile acid biosynthesis, aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis and tryptophan 
metabolism. Correspondingly, 5 different endogenous metabolites were matched with 
metabolism pathways in LPS group, and thus these metabolites were further suggested to be 
serum metabolism indicators of ALI, such as LysoPC (18:2), LPA (18:1), L-histidine, 
taurocholic acid, and L-tryptophan. Furthermore, the analysis of metabolic pathways involved 
in PSG or DEX treatment screened out 6 pathways including aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis, 


 
16 
nitrogen metabolism, histidine metabolism, glycerophospholipid metabolism, tryptophan 
metabolism, arginine and proline metabolism (Figure 4B and 4C).  
It is common to know that pathways with the impact-value above 0.1 were considered as key 
pathways by analyzing the impact factor of the metabolic pathways [30]. In this study, we 
thus focused on the 4 critical pathways among 8 pathways in rats of LPS treated alone, 
including glycerophospholipid metabolism, nitrogen metabolism, histidine metabolism and 
tryptophan metabolism. Nitrogen metabolism, histidine metabolism and tryptophan 
metabolism, were improved in ALI rats by the treatment of PSG, whose impact-values were 
0.11, 0.23 and 0.13, respectively.  
Subsequently, the metabolites involved in the critical pathways were classified into two 
categories: (1) amino acids (AA) and (2) glycerophospholipids. L-histidine, neutral AA, is 
related to nitrogen metabolism and histidine metabolism. Growing evidences have pointed out 
that LPS-induced ALI is a main catabolic insult leading to disturbances of protein metabolism, 
and deranged plasma amino acid patterns [31, 32]. L-histidine was found to increase in 
plasma of ALI in abdominal sepsis rats [33]. L-histidine could be metabolized into histamine 
and urinary acid through deamination and decarboxylation. Basically, histamine is a chemical 
mediator to be implicated in the occurrence and development of inflammatory response [34]. 
The excessive histamine could result in NF-κB activation, which promoted the mRNA 
expression of relevant inflammatory factors, such as TNF-ɑ, IL-1β, IL-1, IL-6 [26, 35]. 
Compared with control group, the level of L-histidine in plasma was significantly increased in 
LPS group, which was significantly reversed by PSG. In contrast, DEX administration 
emerged a further remarkable increase of L-histidine when compared to LPS. Studies have 


 
17 
uncovered that DEX as a glucocorticoid significantly inhibited histamine biosynthesis 
resulting in the increase of L-histidine in LPS treated spleen cells, extend suggested that 
adverse effects of DEX might be related to ruin histamine metabolism. Meanwhile, Williams 
et al. reported that DEX notably increased in the concentration of plasma histidine in infants 
with bronchopulmonary dysplasia, which might be related to catabolic enhancement [36]. 
Tryptophan, an essential amino acid, was metabolized by indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO) 
and tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase (TDO) through methoxyindole and kynurenine pathway. 
Kynurenine, a metabolite belonged to kynurenine pathway, was highly implicated in 
progression of ALI [37]. The disturbance of kynurenine contributed to oxidative stress and 
finally induced apoptosis in lung tissue. Meanwhile, IDO activity could be affected by 
pro-inflammatory stimuli including pro-inflammatory TH1-cytokines such as IFN-γ and 
soluble cytokine receptors [38]. Meanwhile, TDO and kynurenine could be enhanced by 
LPS-induced inflammation as well, thereby forming a vicious circle leading to aberrant 
inflammatory response. In the present study, the level of L-tryptophan increased apparently in 
LPS group, while decreased significantly in PSG group and DEX group. Therefore, these 
findings indicated that the protective effects of PSG against LPS-induced ALI might be 
conducted by mitigating the generation of L-tryptophan in vivo. 
Glycerophospholipids act as the parts of cell membranes and its metabolic disorder is a 
central step during inflammation-related ALI [39, 40]. Our results showed that 
glycerophospholipid accounted for the largest proportion among all the different metabolites 
in relation to the LPS-facilitated ALI in rats. The perturbed glycerophospholipids metabolism 
such as LysoPC (18:2) and LysoPA (18:1) identified in our study, have been recognized to 


 
18 
further induce inflammatory response on ALI via changing energy metabolism and lipid 
metabolism. LysoPC could serve as a chemotactic mediator and participate the inflammation 
process via modification of the activation of immune cells by LPC-specific G-protein-coupled 
receptor [38]. Notably, LysoPC has been shown to inhibit the secretion of proinflammatory 
cytokines in monocytes induced by LPS [42]. Interestingly, the significant decrease of 
LysoPC such as LysoPC (P-18:0) was found in serum of sepsis mice exposed to cecal ligation

3.10 Effect of PSG on SCFAs of Cecum Contents in LPS-treated Rats 
A compelling set of the correlations between the gut microbiota, nutrient digestion, host 
defense and maintenance of immune system have been demonstrated [44, 45]. Moreover, 
studies emerged that ALI could lead to the lung microbiota chaos, induce a transient 
translocation of bacteria into blood and give rise to an acute increase of bacterial load in 
cecum [46, 47]. In particular, studies have suggested that gut microbiota is implicated in the 
immune response in the lung. SCFAs is a main group of microbial metabolites and its chaos 


 
19 
has crucial impacts on various diseases and may alleviate lung injury by correcting the 
leukocyte recruitment and chemokines production by blood flowing. It is generally accepted 
that SCFAs such as acetic, propionic and butyric acids could be linked between microbiota 
and host tissues, and partially mediate inflammation and immune effects in lung [44]. To 
determined the mechanisms on the relationship between gut and lung, SCFAs derived from 
caecal content was identified in this work. Results showed that total SCFAs and individual 
SCFAs (acetic, propionic and butyric acids ) in caecum were notably reduced in LPS rats 
when compared to control rats. After PSG treatment, total SCFAs and individual SCFAs in 
caecum were significantly adjusted to normal levels (p<0.05), which were not observed in the 
DEX (Figure 4D). Extensive work on gut microbiota has confirmed that SCFAs could restrain 
the production of cytokines (IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-ɑ, and NO) and promote the production of 
anti-inﬂammatory cytokine IL-10 by stimulating G-protein couple receptors. Moreover, 
growing studies revealed a critical role for of inflammation by a gut-lung axis, and thus our 
findings supported that the lung-protective effects of PSG could achieved by improving the 
crosstalk between gut and lung via regulation of SCFAs in ALI rats (Figure 5). 
In a word, our findings suggested that PSG exhibited protective effects against ALI by 
inhibiting the inflammatory activities in response to LPS treatment, as evidenced by 
maintaining pulmonary histology, improving WBC count and attenuating immune organ 
indexes. These benefits concomitantly reduced the concentration of TNF-ɑ, IL-6, IL-1β, and 
NO in the serum and lung of rats. Moreover, LysoPC (18:2), LysoPA (18:1), taurocholic acid, 
L-histidine and L-tryptophan which were significantly changed in ALI rats could be as 
biomarkers. The treatment of PSG could remedy LPS-induced ALI by improving histidine 


 
20 
metabolism, nitrogen metabolism, tryptophan and part glycerophospholipids metabolism. 
Finally, PSG could significantly increase the concentrations of acetic, propionic, and butyric 
acids in the cecum. Based on these observations, PSG, a diet polysaccharide, could be 
employed as an alternative dietary supplement or clinical adjuvant to ameliorate ALI. 
Additionally, we revealed that the enhancement of SCFAs was in association with the lung 
benefits of PSG. Further investigations will be necessary to focus on gut–lung axis to reveal 
the immune mechanisms in lung protection of PSG, along with the explanation of biological 
roles of these obtained metabolites.
